A compound can show keto–enol (or analogous) tautomerism only when the carbonyl carbon has at least one sufficiently acidic α-hydrogen that can migrate to the oxygen.  

• 1,3,5-Cyclohexane­trione has CH₂ groups α to each C=O.  Proton transfer from any one of those CH₂ positions to the neighbouring carbonyl oxygen gives an enol; three such shifts generate benzene-1,3,5-triol, an aromatic form strongly favoured over the non-aromatic triketone.  Hence cyclohexane-1,3,5-trione readily undergoes tautomerism.

• In p-benzoquinone each carbonyl carbon is flanked only by vinylic (sp²) carbons.  The hydrogens on those sp² carbons are not acidic enough for ordinary keto-enol interconversion, so benzoquinone does not exhibit tautomerism under normal conditions.

For optical isomerism, a molecule must contain a chiral centre (or another element of chirality) and lack an internal plane of symmetry.

• Methyl 2-hydroxypropanoate (methyl lactate) contains the stereogenic carbon CH(OH)–CO₂Me–CH₃–H; its four different substituents make it chiral, so it exists as a pair of enantiomers.

• Dimethyl fumarate (trans-butenedioate di-methyl ester) has a C₂h symmetry plane passing through the C=C bond and the midpoint of the molecule; it is therefore achiral and does not show optical isomerism.

Thus,
A (does not tautomerise) = benzoquinone  
B (shows optical isomerism) = methyl 2-hydroxypropanoate

Answer: B
